📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in August 2011, Boeing officially launched its 737 MAX program after American Airlines made the historic decision to split its once all-Boeing fleet and buy 50% of its next-generation narrowbodies from Airbus.
  • Recent findings suggest that by mid-2011, Airbus had accumulated more than 1,000 orders for its re-engined A320neo.
  • Sources indicate that modifying the legacy 737 airframe was estimated to cost a third as much, with initial deliveries expected in 2017.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in August 2011, Boeing officially launched its 737 MAX program after American Airlines made the historic decision to split its once all-Boeing fleet and buy 50% of its next-generation narrowbodies from Airbus. AA was facing rising fuel expenses and operating an aging fleet of roughly 300 McDonnell Douglas MD-80 jets. Thus, in July of that same year, AA revealed that of the 460 jets it planned to procure to modernize its fleet, 260 would be from the A320 family.

Recent findings suggest that by mid-2011, Airbus had accumulated more than 1,000 orders for its re-engined A320neo. The airline chose to award more than half of its future fleet slots to Airbus because it already had a production-ready jet. In the aftermath, Boeing leadership abandoned intends for an all-upcoming composite narrowbody within hours. Developing a new mainline jet would have required an estimated $10 billion to $12 billion and up to a decade of research. Instead, it committed to developing a re-engined 737 to retain its portion of the order.

Sources indicate that modifying the legacy 737 airframe was estimated to cost a third as much, with initial deliveries expected in 2017. Boeing also pursued certification as a derivative of the original 1967 type to entice operators with a cheap transition, even earning a $1 million per-aircraft rebate from launch customer Southwest Airlines. However, preserving grandfathered handling characteristics while integrating larger, higher-bypass turbofans onto the low-slung 1960s airframe imposed engineering constraints that forced Boeing to make a fateful compromise: the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System.

In a recent development, at first, Boeing executives James Albaugh and Jim McNerney placed a wager on the Yellowstone Project, believing that airlines would wait for a 2020 clean-sheet composite plane instead of using the Airbus A320neo. Instead, to immediately save 15% on fuel consumption, operators quickly acquired more than 1,000 European narrowbodies. McNerney was then forced to abandon the Yellowstone study over the course of one weekend after American Airlines CEO Gerard Arpey threatened to terminate the airline's exclusive purchase agreement unless Boeing promptly supplied a re-engined 737.

Industry observers note that following the 737 MAX's formal debut on August 30, 2011, commercial contracts obliged Boeing to follow an accelerated derivative timetable. Southwest Airlines, the first client, ordered 150 aircraft in December 2011 under an arrangement that called for a $1 million rebate per plane if regulators imposed pilot simulator training. With Southwest eventually buying over 240 airframes, avoiding hundreds of millions of dollars in penalties necessitated certifying the 737 MAX using its original 1967 type certificate on a tight timetable.

Aerodynamic concessions were necessary to meet that deadline while mounting larger CFM International LEAP-1B engines onto the low-slung 1960s airframe. At high angles of attack, an uncontrollable nose-up pitching tendency was produced by cantilevering the nacelles forward and upward. Engineers used the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System software to digitally mask the pitch anomaly, accelerating delivery while introducing a single-sensor flight control vulnerability, instead of implementing structural wing modifications that would cause certification delays and simulator training.

Boeing engineers had to extend the nose landing gear on the 737 MAX by 8 inches (20 cm) more than the Next Generation series, as well as cantilever the nacelles forward and upward using structural titanium pylons in order to fit 69-inch (175 cm) CFM International LEAP-1B engines onto the low-slung 1967 737 airframe. These larger engine cowls, which were positioned above the wing chord, produced excess aerodynamic lift ahead of the center of gravity at high angles of attack, creating an uncontrollable nose-up pitching tendency that went against federal regulations for linear control column force progression toward an aerodynamic stall.

Recent findings suggest that rather than executing costly structural wing redesigns or installing mechanical counterweights, Boeing relied on the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System software to automatically command nose-down horizontal stabilizer trim without pilot input. To preserve grandfathered type-certificate commonality and avoid simulator training penalties, program officials positioned the software as a minor modification to the existing speed trim system and obtained Federal Aviation Administration approval to strip all references to the system from flight crew manuals, leaving operators and pilots unaware of its existence.

During certification flight testing, Boeing engineers increased the software's ability at lower airspeeds to push the horizontal stabilizer by 2.5 degrees based on input from a single angle-of-attack sensor, without reassessing single-point failure dangers. Boeing withheld internal simulator data from the Federal Aviation Administration, demonstrating that a manufacturer test pilot took more than 10 seconds to diagnose and counter an uncommanded activation, a delay classified as catastrophic internally when compared to the four-second federal response standard.

Recent findings suggest that boeing's Yellowstone Project originally divided commercial fleet renewal into three clean-sheet phases: Y1 for narrowbodies, Y2 for mid-sized jets, and Y3 for widebodies. While Y2 materialized as the composite 787 Dreamliner, severe delays and cost overruns on that program exhausted Boeing's engineering capacity and capital for Y1 and Y3. Simultaneously, Y1 studies stalled when engine manufacturers elected to frame their next-generation turbofans around the A320neo and air carriers ran out of patience, turning to the European planemaker.

Abandoning Y1 for a modified 737 forced engineers to integrate modern high-bypass engines on a fuselage created for 1960s crashworthiness and operating regulations. Grandfathering the type certificate allowed the 737 MAX to use older mechanical flight controls rather than adopt modern fly-by-wire. Thus, engineers could only use software-driven flight controls to a limited extent in compensating for the aircraft's size and weight. Instead, they modified the existing mechanical Speed Trim System with MCAS, using its jackscrew to move the horizontal stabilizer.

This reliance on grandfathered systems created direct performance gaps that a clean-sheet Y1 design would have eliminated through newly introduced systems and certification criteria. Unlike the 787, which features a digital alert system, the 737 MAX retained legacy warning lights and its AOA disagree alert. Disastrously, Boeing engineers discovered in August 2017 that the AOA alert was inoperable on more than 80% of delivered aircraft. Management deferred an MCAS software patch until 2020 and withheld the defect from operators and regulators until after the fatal crash in October 2018 of Lion Air Flight 610.

According to recent reports, to reclaim narrowbody market share lost to the Airbus A320neo, Boeing structured the 737 MAX around minimizing airline transition costs and preserving existing fleet infrastructure. The high-bypass turbofans of the A320neo achieved 15% better fuel efficiency than the 737 NG thanks to large volumes of air around the engine core. Boeing required a very wide front fan diameter on its 737 MAX to match that, a design criterion that clashed with the 737's low ground clearance.

Boeing commercial leadership recognized that any derivative aircraft requiring full-flight simulator sessions would forfeit sales to legacy 737 operators. These commercial imperatives were codified directly into customer purchase agreements, most notably SWA's 240-strong order that included a $1 million rebate per delivered aircraft. Consequently, Boeing set minimal difference training as a core program objective. That meant pilot transition instruction from the 737 NG would be just a computer-based course, avoiding the expense of building and certifying fresh full-flight simulators before service entry.

Thus, to preserve the 1967 type certificate and avoid costly landing gear and wing-box redesigns, CFM International constrained the LEAP-1B to a 69-inch fan (175 cm) and a 9:1 bypass ratio, using 18 carbon-fiber composite blades to reduce rotational mass. Even with a flattened nacelle bottom, fitting the 6,129-pound (2,780 kg) engines required lengthening the nose gear by 8 inches (20 cm) and cantilevering the powerplants forward and upward on titanium pylons.

Positioned ahead of and above the wing chord, these enlarged cowls generated excess aerodynamic lift at high angles of attack, inducing an uncommanded nose-up pitching tendency that violated federal stall-recovery handling standards. Because extensive wing modifications would have invalidated the standing type certificate and triggered mandatory simulator retraining, Boeing engineers compensated digitally through MCAS to command 2.5 degrees of nose-down trim using data from a single external angle-of-attack vane.

The software enabled the airframe to meet certification handling rules on paper, but leadership went on to lobby the FAA to omit the software from flight crew manuals and differences tables, so Boeing could secure Level B training approval to win back airline orders. A conventional runaway stabilizer highlights trim wheel rotation that pilots can recognize and disable. Meanwhile, MCAS was in discrete increments, and omitting the system deprived flight crews of the diagnostic knowledge to distinguish it as the source of a malfunction.

That software reliance was predetermined by 737 sales contracts negotiated years before the prototype flew. Southwest Airlines, the first customer, ordered 150 737 MAX aircraft in December 2011, with the agreement that Boeing would pay a $1 million rebate per jet if the Federal Aviation Administration permitted simple, simulator-based training for pilots migrating from the 737 NG to the MAX. With Southwest eventually buying over 240 airframes, avoiding hundreds of millions of dollars in penalties forced leadership to maintain common type ratings and remove system references from manuals.

It has been revealed that during the initial 737 MAX 8 flight test campaign starting in January 2016, Boeing originally designed the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System to operate exclusively during high-speed, flaps-up wind-up turns. Lift generated by the forward-mounted CFM International LEAP-1B28 nacelles lightened control column forces as angle of attack increased, violating FAA stall characteristic parameters. Subsequently, software authority was extended to lower airspeeds by developers, allowing 2.5 degrees of nose-down horizontal stabilizer trim based on single-sensor AOA input.

In a recent development, in 2017, 737 Chief Technical Pilot Mark Forkner emailed the FAA Seattle Aircraft Evaluation Group requesting permission to remove references to the MCAS from the Flight Crew Operations Manual, unaware of the extended speed range of MCAS authority. In November 2016, Forkner discovered the system activating aggressively at lower airspeeds in simulator testing, claiming he had unknowingly misled regulators. Yet, Boeing officials never briefed the Seattle Aircraft Evaluation Group on the expanded low-speed authority or corrected their earlier operational representations.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service issues at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge.
  • Emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service issues at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a latest initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants….

Emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a fresh initiative involving this small group of employees:.

On 3 November, Emirates introduced a latest initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers….

A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha).

Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

Industry observers note that it goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

Sources indicate that when it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”.

As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”.

I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

Sources indicate that anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

Recent findings suggest that emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”.

It has been revealed that there’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

What do you make of this Emirates initiative?

According to recent reports, I am a predominantly ground based cabin crew manager for a large European airline but also work as supernumerary crew on 2-3 long haul flights per year. Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.
  • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
  • However, I rapidly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

However, I rapidly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

As the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and demonstrated the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically mentioned, “that means nothing.”.

So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

Only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a massive deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

Recent findings suggest that airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

Recent findings suggest that that feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That remarked, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

Sources indicate that even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

Recent findings suggest that inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

Industry observers note that it was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

In a recent development, as for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

It’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of new Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

It has been revealed that if I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….

    Latest Update: End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore.
    • As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.
    • Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

    As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

    Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with latest cabins, including the new business class.

    Still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

    Industry observers note that with this change, no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore either, so it very much is the end of an era. American’s 777 first class seats were controversial — on the one hand, I kind of love how they swivel, though on the other hand, they really lack privacy, and the soft product left a lot to be desired.

    In a recent development, I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

    It’s great that these planes will be getting newly introduced business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

    While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

    In a recent development, specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between Newly introduced York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

    American also plans to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

    American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

    American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and new business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

    In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

    What do you make of the end of American’s Flagship First on the 777?

    Why International First Class Has Failed At US Airlines (But Shouldn’t)

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that we’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore.
    • Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms.
    • Recent findings suggest that airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that we’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

    Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms. This post isn’t about the premium cabin on domestic flights, which is often referred to as first class. Instead, it’s about international flights that have a cabin above business class, when it’s marketed as first class. So this would include airlines on my list of the world’s best first class products.

    Recent findings suggest that airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin. Some insist that there’s no need for such a cabin, as business class has improved so much. Meanwhile others absolutely see merit to such a product.

    I mean, just look at how carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, and SWISS, are all investing in first class. I think Air France’s La Premiere first class is the perfect example of the upside such a product has for an airline:.

    What’s interesting is that for the airlines that succeed with first class, the single biggest market — and single biggest point of sale — is the United States. So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

    The US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

    When they fly first class, they want this….

    It’s no surprise that first class at US carriers has historically failed. In many ways, it reflects the failures of the industry from decades past. In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

    According to recent reports, what explains the failure of first class at US carriers? If you ask me, here are the main factors:.

    Call it a hot take, but I think international first class absolutely could succeed at a US carrier, if done right, with a couple of caveats. Let me start with the two main hurdles that would need to be overcome, and I’ll acknowledge, this might just be the biggest issue:.

    If those hurdles could be overcome, here’s the play, as I see it (and yes, this is largely inspired by Air France La Premiere):.

    It has been revealed that I think the halo effect of something like this would be massive as well. Seriously, US airline executives love to talk about how premium they are, but they can’t even introduce a top-end product, despite having access to the most lucrative customer base in the world.

    In terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:.

    Industry observers note that at this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

    I think no US carrier actually being able to offer a globally competitive product is a failure in strategy and creativity. They have access to the world’s most lucrative customer base, and other airlines can seemingly make money serving US customers with a first class product. The glitch is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

    Industry observers note that personally I think there would be a lot of merit to an international first class product that’s boutique, and is operated in the right markets. That’s not to say that I think it’ll happen — I don’t — but I do think it could succeed. The only real hurdle to overcome would be how to ensure good service….

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images).

    That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

    “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

    Trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he rolled out a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

    “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

    They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

    His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

    Both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

    Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

    In a recent development, “I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump stated as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

    “You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”.

    Trump, who was convicted by a New York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

    According to recent reports, “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump remarked, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

    Other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

    And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of issues, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

    “This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer noted.

    Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”.

    Recent findings suggest that nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He said it was “vital” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”.

    Industry observers note that “The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”.

    Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers mentioned they doubted very much would come from it.

    “I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

    “I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”.

    Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

    “Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal said Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”.

    Recent findings suggest that on spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to promptly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

    Recent findings suggest that “You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”.

    It has been revealed that john M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

    #54047. Tech Report: An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (952 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting.
    • In a recent development, that is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating.
    • The fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “big three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting. Each leader has pronounced himself satisfied with their discussion. But if their concluding statement is an accurate reflection of what was said in the closed session, little of any real consequence — with one possible exception — was agreed to, which was only to be expected. Much has been made by some of the symbolism of the meeting. Did it signal that a disreputable carve-up, even a new Yalta, was underway? If that was the plan, the result, appropriately and mercifully, looks like a package with more than a touch of Temu about it.

    In a recent development, that is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating. Trump’s earlier, overly enthusiastic greeting of his “friend” Putin — the aggressor, after all, in a genocidal war — was not only nauseating but also careless. It sent a disturbing signal to the rest of NATO, an organization that still plays a critical role in maintaining American security as well as peace, however uneasy, in Europe west of Ukraine. It is to be hoped that Trump’s delight at the sight of his supposed pal was, to use a word often applied to this president’s approach to diplomacy, transactional, a display of a dealmaker’s schmooze and nothing more.

    The fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “big three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away. Russia is economically enfeebled and embroiled in a brutally and humiliatingly debilitating war, but it remains a vast, resource-rich country that, militarily anyway, counts as a superpower and one that, as Ukrainians can testify, is still capable of wreaking immense destruction. The more interesting symbolism was detectable in the various gestures through which Xi Jinping emphasized during Putin’s visit that Russia is China’s junior partner. That, too, is today’s reality.

    Industry observers note that as alluded to above, the joint statement issued after the meeting was, as should have been expected, thin gruel. There was talk of reforming the U.N. “so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its fundamental mission of maintaining international peace and security.” If that implies reining in Turtle Bay’s efforts to extend supranational (and thus post-democratic) governance, that’s no bad thing, but in practice little will probably change.

    In a similar vein, the trio, whose countries have not submitted to the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, implicitly criticized the attempted extension of its reach. They stressed the need for “respect for immunities of State officials,” a subject doubtless close to Putin’s heart. There is no need to grumble too much about this. The ICC is highly politicized, and, while it does not constitute much of a deterrent, it may even provide a perverse incentive to wrongdoers to hang onto power. Putin deserves to face judgment, but a better place for that would be Kyiv, not The Hague.

    Industry observers note that and all three declared that they planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.” If that reflected some post-midterms unease on Trump’s part, that, as an admission of weakness, would have been a message better not sent. It would also be a mistake, despite recent waivers, for the U.S. to abandon its general application of sanctions on Iranian and Russian oil (the Europeans, incidentally, could do a better job of enforcing theirs). No pressure should be put on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure other than as part of a general “energy cease-fire” such as that floated earlier this year, which Ukraine was willing to accept.

    No details have been released so far of what was noted in the meeting about Ukraine. However, Putin has been reiterating his hard line, supplemented by an absurd and aggressive proposal to rewrite Europe’s security architecture. Hopefully, Trump was not misled by any bonhomie in Shenzhen, although some accounts of his later call with European leaders were not entirely encouraging in that respect.

    It has been revealed that from left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump participate in a trilateral meeting during the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026.

    According to recent reports, to return to reality: China has no interest in helping end the war in Ukraine, and Russia’s ambitions in Europe are such that the eventual consequences of undermining Kyiv’s ability to resist won’t stop at Ukraine’s borders. Speaking of which, we hope that Trump warned Xi and Putin that the growing intensity of “gray zone” activity, from drones in Leipzig Airport to cyberattacks on both sides of the Atlantic, risks triggering retaliation that could easily spiral into something extremely dangerous.

    Any claims that the Shenzhen meeting has delivered the death blow to the post-1945 order would be overblown, akin to complaining about the murder of a corpse. The postwar settlement has been in flux for decades — Nixon, after all, went to China — a process that has accelerated, along with dramatic shifts in relative global economic and political power, since the Soviet collapse. But although the landscape has changed, Trump should pay more attention to America’s successful management of the (first) Cold War. Alliances matter, deterrence works, strength is rewarded, and aggression by, or sponsored by, hostile powers and their proxies should be contained and, where possible, reversed.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    • In a recent development, I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg.
    • Recent findings suggest that however, to answer the economy vs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their fresh A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

    In a recent development, I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

    Recent findings suggest that however, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

    If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

    The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

    Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

    To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

    Industry observers note that it’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

    Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

    I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

    As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

    After the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and remarked she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

    I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

    In a recent development, in the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

    Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time….

    Sources indicate that I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

    If it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

    Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

    Bilt Seeks An $18 Billion Valuation — The Business Behind Its Jennifer Lopez Concert Goes Far Beyond Rent

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, bilt is reportedly seeking to raise $500 million at an $18 billion valuation.
    • Last week Bilt held a dinner for 400 people in the two thousand year old Egyptian Temple of Dendur inside the Metropolitan Museum of Art, with food led by Thomas Keller and Daniel Boulud and a private Jennifer Lopez concert.
    • Consumers see the side of the business that’s relevant to them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, bilt is reportedly seeking to raise $500 million at an $18 billion valuation. That would be roughly two-thirds higher than the $10.75 billion valuation from its last funding round in 2025. They’re asking investors to back a organization that wants to influence where people eat, shop, travel and spend their time, starting with the relationship it built through paying rent. Last week Bilt held a dinner for 400 people in the two thousand year old Egyptian Temple of Dendur inside the Metropolitan Museum of Art, with food led by Thomas Keller and Daniel Boulud and a private Jennifer Lopez concert. Ken Chenault, Roger Goodell and Barry Sternlicht were some of the business leaders speaking. The event launched their ‘NeighborhoodOS’ platform. And that provides real insight into the actual Bilt business, where rewards are just one piece of it. Jennifer Lopez’s video from the Met performance Consumers see the side of the business that’s relevant to them. Most people won’t ever view it as anything other than rewards for rent, or a credit card, and that’s fine. The merchant side doesn’t need to understand the travel rewards piece, either. But in case you want a window into what’s really going on, here’s an attempt at an explanation. J. Lo held a private concert at this dinner. I often see remarks on Reddit about how Bilt spends money each month on celebrities hosting its Rent Day, basically seeing that transaction as payment to market Bilt to them (or as just wasted money). That misses half of it. Bilt’s CEO explained the J. Lo relationship, “We agreed to help do the relaunch of her newly introduced album.” There’s huge value to the celebrity in being featured in front of Bilt’s audience. The financial terms probably vary with each one, but Bilt gains attention from the celebrity and the celebrity gains access to Bilt’s audience. You often see celebrities with something to promote, like J. Lo’s new album. We naturally see ourselves as the customers being rewarded. Our attention and spending are also what Bilt brings to its partners. That’s how it can negotiate rewards for us. Businesses spend money trying to reach customers, and a rewards program returns some of that money to the people whose business they’re trying to attract. The scale of Bilt’s ambitions are pretty massive. Bilt is trying to eat the world. Or at least a meaningful share of the $6.6 trillion in annual U.S. retail and food services spending it says happens in person. Their business began with a really insightful way to find good customers – reach into their homes, process their rent and get them signed up. Bilt’s latest company announcement says its platform reaches approximately one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. They report more than 8.2 million members and over $12 billion in rewarded spending at local merchants over the past year. Rewarded spending isn’t necessarily spending Bilt caused, but it’s a substantial base of transactions to build their platform off us. As I wrote earlier this year, move-in is a particularly valuable moment. Someone needs a coffee shop, gym, pharmacy and regular place for dinner. Their habits are up for grabs. Acquiring that relationship through their home gives Bilt a chance to influence years of spending. The early audience was especially attractive. In a 2024 interview, its head of loyalty Dave Canty (ex-Starwood, IHG, JetBlue) described core customers aged 24–34, a median age around 29 and average income around $147,000. That made it easier to sign on initial partners who wanted access to the young professionals Bilt was reaching. Airlines start with people who want their miles already sitting on their planes. An independent rewards program has to find its own reason for customers to join. Bilt found one in an expense nearly everyone has, and where there wasn’t competition in offering rewards for their transactions. They offered property owners stickiness as well as a better payment processing platform. American Express’s Plenti had major merchants and their customers, but never established a compelling enough new relationship to change spending. It closed in 2018. Coalition rewards have achieved some scale abroad, including Air Miles in Canada and Nectar in Britain. The challenge is making the common program worth choosing over whatever customers already do. Bilt has better tools for that than a small rebate. I consider its points the most valuable transferable currency. A restaurant’s standalone rewards might never accumulate into anything I care about. Combine them with points from housing and other spending, and they can contribute to a Hyatt stay or an international business class award. A restaurant wants nearby customers who spend well and return. It also needs to handle reservations, remember guests, deliver good service and get paid without wasting staff time. Neighborhood OS connects systems the restaurant already uses. OpenTable’s new partnership puts guest information into its table management system and brings personalized offers into the OpenTable app. The restaurant can send an offers to people who’ve just moved nearby and manage offers for regulars – their own loyalty platform. OpenTable reports that participating restaurants have seen: Average checks up to 18% higher among Bilt members than other guests. Table turns reduced by up to 11 minutes on average. Higher average bills may be Bilt’s customer base being higher spending, or they may be encouraging higher spend. That’s not clear. But their technology does seem to speed up paying and leaving, which means serving more guests per table. Bilt’s mobile checkout lets diners tap or scan a receipt card, view the check, split it and pay in a browser. You can leave when you’re finished without waiting for someone to take your credit card and bring it back. Removing dead time after a meal gives the guest back their evening and makes the table available sooner. When there’s demand for another seating, a restaurant can generate more revenue from the same space. Keller and Boulud’s involvement extends beyond preparing food for a launch dinner. In Bilt’s March hospitality announcement, Keller described learning who guests are before they arrive. Boulud talked about inviting wine enthusiasts to wine events and cocktail enthusiasts to cocktail events. Connecting reservations, preferences, past visits and payments helps a restaurant recognize more people than an owner can personally remember. The restaurant can also deliver an experience through other Bilt partners. At Block’s investor day last year, Bilt’s President and Chief Revenue Officer Brandt Smallwood described automating drinks after a third visit, as well as benefits such as dessert or a free Lyft ride at the end of the meal. A ride home can be part of the restaurant’s hospitality, with Bilt doing the work connecting the businesses. The customer doesn’t need to understand the systems behind it. They get recognized, something arrives at their table, and their ride is arranged. That’s different from getting an email with a coupon code to remember next time. There’s also less work for employees. A Google Cloud case study describes Bilt’s concierge moving a reservation and adjusting party size through the underlying systems. It reports about 95% of member conversations handled without a human handoff, up from 86% six months earlier. More partners also means more ways to fund the benefits.     #54043. Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (959 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop.
    • It has been revealed that however, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick.
    • On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

    It has been revealed that however, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

    On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

    It has been revealed that the plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then promptly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

    After the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

    Recent findings suggest that once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

    There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

    A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

    What explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

    In other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

    Industry observers note that in this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

    However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

    In a recent development, so while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety glitch. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

    Sources indicate that A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

    Sources indicate that while this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety issue, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

    What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.     It has been revealed that rove is launching personalized shopping offers of up to 25 miles per dollar on November 20. Connect your card accounts, activate an offer, and the program can give you a higher earning rate based on your shopping history.

    It has been revealed that if you buy from Nike, Adidas may be willing to spend real money to win your next purchase. That’s the example I reported from Rove’s presentation at the oneworld Loyalty Summit in September. CEO Max Morganroth described targeted merchant commissions reaching 40%. This puts that pitch in front of consumers, with an established advertising tech giant helping supply the offers.

    Sources indicate that rove claims members will find personalized offers in the ‘For You’ section of its website and app after connecting their card accounts. Enhanced offers will display the standard earning rate alongside the higher rate.

    It has been revealed that they’re also expanding in-store earning to hundreds of participating physical retailers. Activate an eligible offer before buying, pay with the connected card, and the purchase gets tracked when the charge clears. Rove indicates miles will typically post within seven days.

    These are selected offers reaching up to 25x, and Rove tells me merchants can change from month to month, and the same merchant might offer one person 5x and another 20x depending on whom it wants to reach.

    Rove began rolling out in-store shopping alongside its app, dining program and instant gift card rewards in August. The newly introduced pieces are the personalized enhanced rates and broader retail coverage.

    A shopping portal generally earns a commission for sending a merchant a sale. Better targeting can make that referral worth more.

    Someone who regularly spends money in a category, but buys from a competitor, is a prospect worth reaching. So is someone who used to shop at a store and stopped. A merchant might pay to bring that person back, get an occasional customer to make another visit, or encourage a larger purchase.

    Recent findings suggest that the best prospect isn’t necessarily the biggest spender. It’s the person whose spending the offer can profitably change. Adidas gains little from paying a committed Adidas customer a huge rebate on shoes they were already going to buy. And it doesn’t much from showing a Nike loyalist an offer they’ll never use.

    Sources indicate that rewards provider Valuedynamx describes a retailer campaign that gave new shoppers stronger incentives, lapsed shoppers offers to bring them back, and loyal customers smaller rewards.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S.
    • Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a newly introduced challenge: Attendance.
    • Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, said attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a newly introduced challenge: Attendance.

    Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-reveals – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

    It has been revealed that the House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

    In a recent development, "Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members.".

    “We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

    Of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-shows; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

    Sources indicate that johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

    “I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, said. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”.

    And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

    Sources indicate that “There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

    “I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan said. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”.

    Attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

    While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

    Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

    However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

    In a recent development, “The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., said. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”.
