    Why JSX Just Bought Newly introduced Pacific Airlines, The Strange, Failed 757 Startup

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired New Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.
    • If you’re not familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.
    • It has been revealed that let’s start with a little context.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired New Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.

    If you’re not familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.

    It has been revealed that let’s start with a little context. JSX is a public charter air carrier, which operates a fleet of nearly 60 planes, most of which are Embraer E135s and E145s.

    It operates as a Part 135 operator, meaning it’s not technically an airline, as it’s using a loophole that allows it to not use standard TSA security screening, hire pilots with fewer than 1,500 hours, etc. Basically what’s happening is that one subsidiary sells the tickets, and then another subsidiary operates the flights, so it’s technically a “charter” (with 30 people who don’t know one another).

    Recent findings suggest that then there’s Latest Pacific Airlines, one of the strangest airline startups we’ve ever seen, and which I’ve covered extensively. The airline acquired some Boeing 757s, and the business strategy was to connect North America and Asia via Anchorage (ANC).

    Industry observers note that the business model made zero sense in the first place, though there was some funding there, and they even invested in constructing a lounge in Anchorage, even though those flights never did happen. The airline did briefly fly from (ONT) to Nashville (BNA) — as one does — before ultimately going out of business.

    According to recent reports, that brings us to the news. New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with Embraer E145s that are leased from JSX, as reported by IshrionA. According to a Department of Transportation filing, the airline intends to resume flights with planes featuring 42 seats, which is higher than the 30-seat limit you’ll find on current JSX planes.

    JSX acquires Newly introduced Pacific Airlines.New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with ERJ 145 leased from JSX. pic.twitter.com/uMMS0J2fZy.

    According to recent reports, on the surface, this of course makes absolutely no sense. New Pacific Airlines was out of business, and the business model made no sense. So why would JSX buy an airline and then lease planes to it?

    In a recent development, long story short, this seems to be a play to acquire a cheap Part 121 certificate. A Part 121 operator is a organization that’s allowed to operate scheduled air transport… in other words, a “real” airline. As I mentioned above, JSX has historically been a Part 135 operator, and that explicitly means it’s not an airline. It’s a public charter air carrier, so it’s not a “real” airline.

    Going back a couple of years, we know that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was considering cracking down on carriers like JSX, since they definitely don’t operate within the spirit of the rules. That’s not to say that JSX did anything wrong, because by the letter of the law, they’re following it exactly. It’s just that the letter of the law makes no sense, and clearly doesn’t reflect the intent behind distinguishing between Part 121 and Part 135 operators.

    Recent findings suggest that under Trump, there was no scrutiny of this. However, with Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, I imagine JSX leaders may be worried that there could again be more scrutiny. If nothing else, buying a cheap Part 121 certificate is a good insurance policy, in case the government does crack down. After all, these can basically be “sold,” while acquiring one from scratch can be grueling process.

    I wouldn’t assume that anything will really operate with Newly introduced Pacific Airlines branding, or based on a New Pacific Airlines business model. Instead, I imagine the idea is that JSX will start dabbling in Part 121 operations, which is why these planes will have more seats (above the 30-seat cap that’s allowed), since that’s no longer a factor.

    If the government were to crack down on Part 135 operators, JSX could move to Part 121 operations. However, they’d have to make lots of changes, from their pilot hiring, to the way passengers are screened.

    According to recent reports, JSX has just bought New Pacific, the airline with an absurd business model that went bankrupt. No, JSX isn’t inspired by the concept of flying Boeing 757s to Asia. Instead, this is clearly the cheapest way for JSX to acquire a Part 121 certificate, which would be required for the carrier to continue operations in the event that the government were to crack down on the Part 135 operator loophole.

    It’s going to be interesting to see how this evolves, both since JSX seems to have aims to operate Part 121 operations in the near future, and also to see how JSX’s business model would evolve if the Part 135 concept were blocked.

    What do you make of this JSX Part 121 play?

Instead, she was escorted off the roughly 9 p.m. flight to Boise and quoted about $400 for a departure the next morning. Southwest was right about the Companion Pass rule. Surely though it shouldn’t take materially longer to sell a ticket than to remove a passenger. She’d spent four days in Las Vegas, checked two 50 pound bags, and was ready to get home. Sitting in row 14, she’d already given the flight attendant her verbal agreement to help with the emergency exit. Her headphones were on. She was listening to an audiobook and playing a game on her phone. Then came the announcement asking Mr. Batis to identify himself. She told the crew he wasn’t on board and wouldn’t be joining them. That’s when she realized why the middle seat was empty. An employee came back to her row and explained that her free ticket depended on her husband actually taking the flight. She says he told her they were ready to push back. He left, returned about three minutes later, and told her she’d have to get off. She gathered her things and went with him. I think he was expecting, like, some complete chaos. @angiebatis — Her account of being removed from the Southwest flight Companion Pass Requires The Passholder To Travel I’ve been a Companion Pass holder, including through promotions, and it’s still an extraordinary deal. Book your own Southwest flight with money or points, then add your designated companion for taxes and fees starting at $5.60 each way, as long as there’s a seat available. The free travel is tied to accompanying the passholder. Her husband paid for a ticket, which then supports the companion’s ticket. The rules though are very clear: If the Companion is not traveling with the Member, the Companion’s reservation will be canceled. I’ve covered almost this exact situation before. In June 2024, a companion boarded Southwest flight 2097 from Savannah to Baltimore. The passholder canceled his own ticket just before departure. Southwest removed the companion, conducting a manual boarding pass check to find her in the days before assigned seating. That case involved a cancellation and an apparent attempt to get the companion transported while refunding the underlying ticket. Here the passenger was fully willing to pay. I don’t think she was actually trying to scam the airline, though she’d be traveling free (and if her husband did cancel in time prior to departure he’d still have his flight credit to use). The requirement to fly together isn’t one of the changes Southwest is making to Companion Pass in 2027. It’s been a longstanding requirement. She Offered To Pay For The Seat Comments on the woman’s video between people who think a longtime Southwest customer should know how the pass works and people who think the airline should have found a way to get her home. It’s probably just best that she got off without making a scene. Several viewers ask why this wasn’t caught at check-in or at the gate. But checking in isn’t the same as boarding. If her husband wasn’t checked in though it should get caught at the check-in deadline. He may have been checked in and just didn’t board. There’s an interesting bit of history here. In this video, she also thanks the gate agent and tells her it isn’t her fault. Her host at the Venetian arranged a chauffeur, another room, dinner and a car back to the airport.     Angie Batis says she offered to buy her own ticket, using a credit card or points, but was told it was too late. Instead, she was escorted off the roughly 9 p.m. flight to Boise and quoted about $400 for a departure the next morning. Southwest was right about the Companion Pass rule. Surely though it shouldn’t take materially longer to sell a ticket than to remove a passenger.

    Industry observers note that she’d spent four days in Las Vegas, checked two 50 pound bags, and was ready to get home. Sitting in row 14, she’d already given the flight attendant her verbal agreement to help with the emergency exit. Her headphones were on. She was listening to an audiobook and playing a game on her phone.

    Then came the announcement asking Mr. Batis to identify himself. She told the crew he wasn’t on board and wouldn’t be joining them. That’s when she realized why the middle seat was empty.

    Industry observers note that an employee came back to her row and explained that her free ticket depended on her husband actually taking the flight. Well, can I just pay with a credit card? … I’ve been a Southwest card member for 20 plus years. I have my own points. Can I just book it, you know, pay for it now? She claims he told her they were ready to push back. He left, returned about three minutes later, and told her she’d have to get off. She gathered her things and went with him. I think he was expecting, like, some complete chaos. @angiebatis — Her account of being removed from the Southwest flight Companion Pass Requires The Passholder To Travel I’ve been a Companion Pass holder, including through promotions, and it’s still an extraordinary deal. Book your own Southwest flight with money or points, then add your designated companion for taxes and fees starting at $5.60 each way, as long as there’s a seat available. The free travel is tied to accompanying the passholder. Her husband paid for a ticket, which then supports the companion’s ticket. The rules though are very clear: If the Companion is not traveling with the Member, the Companion’s reservation will be canceled. I’ve covered almost this exact situation before. In June 2024, a companion boarded Southwest flight 2097 from Savannah to Baltimore. The passholder canceled his own ticket just before departure. Southwest removed the companion, conducting a manual boarding pass check to find her in the days before assigned seating. That case involved a cancellation and an apparent attempt to get the companion transported while refunding the underlying ticket. Here the passenger was fully willing to pay. I don’t think she was actually trying to scam the airline, though she’d be traveling free (and if her husband did cancel in time prior to departure he’d still have his flight credit to use). The requirement to fly together isn’t one of the changes Southwest is making to Companion Pass in 2027. It’s been a longstanding requirement. She Offered To Pay For The Seat Comments on the woman’s video between people who think a longtime Southwest customer should know how the pass works and people who think the airline should have found a way to get her home. It’s probably just best that she got off without making a scene. Several viewers ask why this wasn’t caught at check-in or at the gate. But checking in isn’t the same as boarding.     #54036. Breaking: Bilt Offers JetBlue Elite Status For December Rent Day—With A Fast Track To Keep It Through 2027

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 50m • 📚 Deep Dive (10014 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Bilt Offers JetBlue Elite Status For December Rent Day—With A Fast Track To Keep It Through 2027

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 50 min read (10014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~50 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that bilt’s December Rent Day offers a three month trial of JetBlue elite status, with a much easier path to keeping it through January 2028.
    • When Bilt added JetBlue as a transfer partner last month, I wrote that status matches could be coming.
    • There’s also up to a 100% bonus redeeming Bilt points for credit card statement credits, a targeted spending offer, and Brittany Snow playing Rent Free.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that bilt’s December Rent Day offers a three month trial of JetBlue elite status, with a much easier path to keeping it through January 2028. Silver and Gold members get Mosaic 1 at no points cost. Platinum members start at Mosaic 2, which means EvenMore seats at booking instead of waiting until closer to departure. When Bilt added JetBlue as a transfer partner last month, I wrote that status matches could be coming. You qualify based on your Bilt status, so you don’t need to bring elite status from another airline. There’s also up to a 100% bonus redeeming Bilt points for credit card statement credits, a targeted spending offer, and Brittany Snow playing Rent Free. I have no idea who she is. I’m much more interested in the JetBlue offer than cashing out Bilt points at under 1.5 cents apiece. Three Months Of JetBlue Status, With A Path Through January 2028 Here’s the initial status offered: Bilt Status   JetBlue Trial Status   Points Requirement Blue Mosaic 1 10,000 Bilt points Silver Mosaic 1 None Gold Mosaic 1 None Platinum Mosaic 2 None Blue members have to transfer 10,000 points to trigger the match. Everyone has three months after receiving the matched status to earn and receive enough qualifying tiles to extend it through January 31, 2028: Status Earned   Challenge Requirement   Normal Annual Requirement Mosaic 1 10 tiles 50 tiles Mosaic 2 25 tiles 100 tiles Mosaic 3 40 tiles 150 tiles Under JetBlue’s normal earning rules, a tile takes $100 in qualifying spending on flights, JetBlue Vacations or TrueBlue Travel, or $1,000 in JetBlue credit card spending. So the travel equivalents are $1,000, $2,500 and $4,000. Taxes and fees don’t count. The corresponding spend amounts would be $10,000, $25,000 and $40,000, or you could combine tiles from travel and card spending. Spending on a Bilt card isn’t JetBlue card spending. You can earn JetBlue tiles via travel on JetBlue, United Airlines, JetBlue Vacations; cobrand card spend; purchased or earned bonus tiles (but gifted tiles don’t count); and the annual 25 Tile Bonus awarded to JetBlue Premier Wcardmembers. Folks who have received a past JetBlue challenge are eligible for this offer. Where The Status Is Most Useful The immediate value is better seating and fewer fees on trips you already intend to take. Mosaic 1 includes one checked bag, priority services, eligible same-day switches, and complimentary EvenMore selection starting 36 hours before departure for the member and up to two companions, subject to availability. Mosaic 2 adds a second checked bag and moves EvenMore selection to booking for the member and up to two companions. Mosaic 3 includes four Premium Upgrade Certificates, the new name for Move to Mint certificates (and those meeting the challenge requirements will receive them). Main Base fares exclude crucial seating benefits. And Mosaic 1 through 3 don’t include Mosaic 4 lounge access. JetBlue has also confirmed complimentary upgrades to its new BlueFirst domestic first class for all Mosaic tiers as equipped aircraft enter service. These are space available upgrades, with higher Mosaic levels ahead of lower ones. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares don’t qualify. Premium Upgrade Certificates can confirm Mint or BlueFirst, including on eligible TrueBlue points tickets. Four certificates don’t necessarily mean four upgrades because the number required varies by flight. Starting February 1, JetBlue will also let Mosaic 2 members select a certificate through Perks You Pick. I’ve asked whether matched members get that selection. There’s A United Airlines Angle, Too Under JetBlue’s Blue Sky partnership, Mosaic members receive benefits on eligible United Airlines trips booked through JetBlue, including a checked bag, preferred seats after booking and Economy Plus at check-in. Mosaic 1 gets Group 2 boarding, while Mosaic 2 and above get Group 1. United flights booked through JetBlue also earn tiles under the ordinary program. So you can keep JetBlue status through travel on United. There’s No Transfer Bonus Bilt points transfer to JetBlue at 1:1. This December announcement doesn’t include a bonus on those transfers. I’m generally not moving Bilt points to JetBlue for ordinary redemptions worth around 1.3 cents apiece. One option worth comparing is a regular paid JetBlue ticket purchased through Bilt’s portal using points. Under ordinary revenue-ticket rules, that should earn tiles, whereas transferring points into TrueBlue doesn’t earn tiles. Portal bookings do give up JetBlue’s direct-booking points bonus. The more interesting transfer uses remain partner business class awards, such as the 54,000-point Condor business class awards from the East Coast to Frankfurt I’ve covered, when available. Mosaic doesn’t add benefits to a Condor flight. If you already have the JetBlue Premier card, its 15% award rebate includes partner flights. A 54,000-point award returns 8,100 TrueBlue points, for a net cost of 45,900. You need all 54,000 upfront, and the rebate comes back as JetBlue points, not Bilt points. A 100% Statement Credit Bonus Still Only Gets You About 1.1 Cents Eligible cardholders get increased statement credit redemption value from November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern through December 2 at 2:59 a.m. Eastern. The minimum redemption is 1,000 points. This bonus depends on which Bilt credit card you have, not your Bilt elite status. At the usual 0.55-cent statement credit redemption rate, the math is: Bilt Card   Bonus   Value Per Point   Credit For 10,000 Points Blue 25% 0.6875 cents $68.75 Obsidian 50% 0.825 cents $82.50 Palladium 100% 1.1 cents $110 I wouldn’t do this. Even Palladium’s doubled rate is less than the $125 in travel those same 10,000 points buy through Bilt, before considering Hyatt or airline transfers. I passed on last month’s gift card bonus, too. Two Separate Opportunities To Earn 1,000 Extra Points Some cardholders will receive a targeted offer for 1,000 bonus points after $500 in everyday purchases from November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern through November 30 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern. Rent and mortgage payments don’t count. Check your account for eligibility. Then the usual Rent Day double points apply on December 1, with a cap of 1,000 additional points: Bilt Blue: 2 points per dollar on everyday spending. Bilt Obsidian: 6 points in your selected dining or grocery category, 4 on travel and 2 on other everyday spending. Bilt Palladium: 4 points per dollar on everyday spending. Rent and tax payments don’t qualify for the extra points (tax payments usually don’t earn at all). On Palladium, $500 in eligible December 1 spending earns the full 1,000-point Rent Day bonus on top of the usual 1,000 points. The holiday shopping offer ends the night before Rent Day. The same purchase can’t satisfy both offers. A targeted Palladium member with $500 of ordinary spending before the deadline and another $500 on December 1 could earn 2,000 promotional bonus points across the two. Brittany Snow, Free Rent And December Experiences Brittany Snow is this month’s Rent Free guest. The game opens November 20 at noon Eastern and closes December 1 at 3 p.m. Eastern, with results after 4 p.m. The top 10 members win a month’s rent up to $2,500, with additional rent winners depending on how well she does. Rent winners also get a signed copy of September Letters. The next 100 receive 1,000 points and the next 500 receive 100 points. There’s also a November 22 brunch with Snow and September Letters co-founder Jaspre Guest at The Twenty Two in New York, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. It’s $45 or 3,000 points, includes bites and cocktails, and opens for booking November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern. Guests must be at least 21. The booking is final sale. The book itself is $20 or 2,000 points, with 100 copies available beginning November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern. Members can apply up to $20 of their monthly Bilt Cash allowance. I’d use available Bilt Cash rather than redeem points at a penny each. Shipping is expected in two to three weeks, and sales are final. Members can write letters through the app, choosing whether to keep them private or share them. Select Bilt Alliance buildings will also have September Letters mailboxes, with letters mailed back to their writers in a year. Bookings for the following experiences open Saturday, November 21 at 11:50 a.m. Eastern for Gold and Platinum, and noon for everyone else: Dining: December 1 meals at 40 restaurants across nine cities. Most cost $35–$78 or 2,500–5,000 points. There are three-course menus at most venues, four courses at Hutong and omakase at seven Bondi locations. Drink add-ons cost $20–$46 and must be purchased when booking. Up to $50 Bilt Cash can be applied to one dining experience, with the rest paid in cash. Book by November 30 at 5 p.m. Eastern. There’s also first access to American Cut’s December 31 cocktail party in New York at 6 p.m., priced at $250, with 20 seats. Comedy: 20 highlights December 4–19. Club experiences cost $40 or 2,500 points, except Mic Drop MANIA in Chandler at $30 or 2,000 points, with two drinks included. Premium experiences cost $75 or 5,000 points and include two drinks and light bites. Austin’s The Creek & The Cave is among the venues. Members can use up to $50 Bilt Cash toward a comedy show for the month. Booking closes at 11 a.m. Eastern on the show date, or when sold out. Fitness: Free December 1 SoulCycle and Barry’s classes, with 1,175 and 580 spots respectively. Bookings close November 30 at 7 p.m. Eastern. Dining allows four seats per member per booking, and comedy allows four tickets per person. These experiences are final sale. I’d use Bilt Cash before points: a common $60 dinner costs 4,000 points, but applying $50 Bilt Cash leaves $10 to pay and keeps your points available for travel. And on December 1, Bilt’s cafe at 837 Washington Street in New York will offer members a complimentary Daniel Boulud tasting from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern: lobster vol-au-vent (with a vegetarian option), warm apple chausson, a hot chocolate shake and warm spiced cider. Topics on this pageBilt RewardsFrequent-flyer programJetBlueTrueBlueCondorFrankfurtHyattNew YorkPremium economy classSnowUnited Airlines+7 more More From View from the Wing.

    Here’s the initial status offered:.

    Blue members have to transfer 10,000 points to trigger the match. Everyone has three months after receiving the matched status to earn and receive enough qualifying tiles to extend it through January 31, 2028:.

    Under JetBlue’s normal earning rules, a tile takes $100 in qualifying spending on flights, JetBlue Vacations or TrueBlue Travel, or $1,000 in JetBlue credit card spending. So the travel equivalents are $1,000, $2,500 and $4,000. Taxes and fees don’t count.

    According to recent reports, the corresponding spend amounts would be $10,000, $25,000 and $40,000, or you could combine tiles from travel and card spending. Spending on a Bilt card isn’t JetBlue card spending.

    Recent findings suggest that you can earn JetBlue tiles via travel on JetBlue, United Airlines, JetBlue Vacations; cobrand card spend; purchased or earned bonus tiles (but gifted tiles don’t count); and the annual 25 Tile Bonus awarded to JetBlue Premier Wcardmembers. Folks who have received a past JetBlue challenge are eligible for this offer.

    Sources indicate that the immediate value is better seating and fewer fees on trips you already intend to take. Mosaic 1 includes one checked bag, priority services, eligible same-day switches, and complimentary EvenMore selection starting 36 hours before departure for the member and up to two companions, subject to availability. Mosaic 2 adds a second checked bag and moves EvenMore selection to booking for the member and up to two companions. Mosaic 3 includes four Premium Upgrade Certificates, the new name for Move to Mint certificates (and those meeting the challenge requirements will receive them). Main Base fares exclude important seating benefits. And Mosaic 1 through 3 don’t include Mosaic 4 lounge access. JetBlue has also announced complimentary upgrades to its new BlueFirst domestic first class for all Mosaic tiers as equipped aircraft enter service. These are space available upgrades, with higher Mosaic levels ahead of lower ones. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares don’t qualify. Premium Upgrade Certificates can confirm Mint or BlueFirst, including on eligible TrueBlue points tickets. Four certificates don’t necessarily mean four upgrades because the number required varies by flight. Starting February 1, JetBlue will also let Mosaic 2 members select a certificate through Perks You Pick. I’ve asked whether matched members get that selection. There’s A United Airlines Angle, Too Under JetBlue’s Blue Sky partnership, Mosaic members receive benefits on eligible United Airlines trips booked through JetBlue, including a checked bag, preferred seats after booking and Economy Plus at check-in. Mosaic 1 gets Group 2 boarding, while Mosaic 2 and above get Group 1. United flights booked through JetBlue also earn tiles under the ordinary program. So you can keep JetBlue status through travel on United. There’s No Transfer Bonus Bilt points transfer to JetBlue at 1:1. This December announcement doesn’t include a bonus on those transfers. I’m generally not moving Bilt points to JetBlue for ordinary redemptions worth around 1.3 cents apiece. One option worth comparing is a regular paid JetBlue ticket purchased through Bilt’s portal using points. Under ordinary revenue-ticket rules, that should earn tiles, whereas transferring points into TrueBlue doesn’t earn tiles. Portal bookings do give up JetBlue’s direct-booking points bonus. The more interesting transfer uses remain partner business class awards, such as the 54,000-point Condor business class awards from the East Coast to Frankfurt I’ve covered, when available. Mosaic doesn’t add benefits to a Condor flight. If you already have the JetBlue Premier card, its 15% award rebate includes partner flights. A 54,000-point award returns 8,100 TrueBlue points, for a net cost of 45,900. You need all 54,000 upfront, and the rebate comes back as JetBlue points, not Bilt points. A 100% Statement Credit Bonus Still Only Gets You About 1.1 Cents Eligible cardholders get increased statement credit redemption value from November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern through December 2 at 2:59 a.m. Eastern. The minimum redemption is 1,000 points. This bonus depends on which Bilt credit card you have, not your Bilt elite status. At the usual 0.55-cent statement credit redemption rate, the math is: Bilt Card   Bonus   Value Per Point   Credit For 10,000 Points Blue 25% 0.6875 cents $68.75 Obsidian 50% 0.825 cents $82.50 Palladium 100% 1.1 cents $110 I wouldn’t do this. Even Palladium’s doubled rate is less than the $125 in travel those same 10,000 points buy through Bilt, before considering Hyatt or airline transfers. I passed on last month’s gift card bonus, too. Two Separate Opportunities To Earn 1,000 Extra Points Some cardholders will receive a targeted offer for 1,000 bonus points after $500 in everyday purchases from November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern through November 30 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern. Rent and mortgage payments don’t count. Check your account for eligibility. Then the usual Rent Day double points apply on December 1, with a cap of 1,000 additional points: Bilt Blue: 2 points per dollar on everyday spending. Bilt Obsidian: 6 points in your selected dining or grocery category, 4 on travel and 2 on other everyday spending. Bilt Palladium: 4 points per dollar on everyday spending. Rent and tax payments don’t qualify for the extra points (tax payments usually don’t earn at all). On Palladium, $500 in eligible December 1 spending earns the full 1,000-point Rent Day bonus on top of the usual 1,000 points. The holiday shopping offer ends the night before Rent Day. The same purchase can’t satisfy both offers. A targeted Palladium member with $500 of ordinary spending before the deadline and another $500 on December 1 could earn 2,000 promotional bonus points across the two. Brittany Snow, Free Rent And December Experiences Brittany Snow is this month’s Rent Free guest. The game opens November 20 at noon Eastern and closes December 1 at 3 p.m. Eastern, with results after 4 p.m. The top 10 members win a month’s rent up to $2,500, with additional rent winners depending on how well she does. Rent winners also get a signed copy of September Letters. The next 100 receive 1,000 points and the next 500 receive 100 points. There’s also a November 22 brunch with Snow and September Letters co-founder Jaspre Guest at The Twenty Two in New York, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. It’s $45 or 3,000 points, includes bites and cocktails, and opens for booking November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern. Guests must be at least 21. The booking is final sale. The book itself is $20 or 2,000 points, with 100 copies available beginning November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern. Members can apply up to $20 of their monthly Bilt Cash allowance. I’d use available Bilt Cash rather than redeem points at a penny each. Shipping is expected in two to three weeks, and sales are final. Members can write letters through the app, choosing whether to keep them private or share them. Select Bilt Alliance buildings will also have September Letters mailboxes, with letters mailed back to their writers in a year. Bookings for the following experiences open Saturday, November 21 at 11:50 a.m. Eastern for Gold and Platinum, and noon for everyone else: Dining: December 1 meals at 40 restaurants across nine cities. Most cost $35–$78 or 2,500–5,000 points. There are three-course menus at most venues, four courses at Hutong and omakase at seven Bondi locations. Drink add-ons cost $20–$46 and must be purchased when booking. Up to $50 Bilt Cash can be applied to one dining experience, with the rest paid in cash. Book by November 30 at 5 p.m. Eastern. There’s also first access to American Cut’s December 31 cocktail party in New York at 6 p.m., priced at $250, with 20 seats. Comedy: 20 reveals December 4–19. Club experiences cost $40 or 2,500 points, except Mic Drop MANIA in Chandler at $30 or 2,000 points, with two drinks included. Premium experiences cost $75 or 5,000 points and include two drinks and light bites. Austin’s The Creek & The Cave is among the venues. Members can use up to $50 Bilt Cash toward a comedy show for the month. Booking closes at 11 a.m. Eastern on the show date, or when sold out. Fitness: Free December 1 SoulCycle and Barry’s classes, with 1,175 and 580 spots respectively. Bookings close November 30 at 7 p.m. Eastern. Dining allows four seats per member per booking, and comedy allows four tickets per person. These experiences are final sale. I’d use Bilt Cash before points: a common $60 dinner costs 4,000 points, but applying $50 Bilt Cash leaves $10 to pay and keeps your points available for travel. And on December 1, Bilt’s cafe at 837 Washington Street in New York will offer members a complimentary Daniel Boulud tasting from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern: lobster vol-au-vent (with a vegetarian option), warm apple chausson, a hot chocolate shake and warm spiced cider.     American Airlines Hasn’t Flown To Israel Since October 7—Now It’s Partnering With The Airline Flying Its Old Jets

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that american Airlines hasn’t flown to Israel since the October 7, 2023 attacks.
    • In a recent development, in August I flagged that Israir had acquired American’s old aircraft.
    • Israir right now flies five times a week between New York JFK and Tel Aviv.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that american Airlines hasn’t flown to Israel since the October 7, 2023 attacks. Israir is flying the route using two of American’s retired Airbus A330s. Now American is partnering with Israir to connect those passengers to its network beyond New York. In August I flagged that Israir had acquired American’s old aircraft. Now it’s getting access to more of the customers it needs to fill those planes. American, meanwhile, gets connecting passengers and an Israeli sales partner ahead of its own planned return to the Israel market. Israir right now flies five times a week between New York JFK and Tel Aviv. American aims to resume daily service March 27, 2027, using Boeing 777-200ERs. I’d covered their previous blueprint to return in March 2026, they’ve kept planning to return and then not, given instability in the region even as other U.S. carriers flew. Ex-American Airlines Airbus A330-200 N287AY, Credit: Anna Zvereva / Wikimedia Commons. What American And Israir Have Agreed To The initial arrangement has two parts: Israir will put its flight code on American’s JFK–Tel Aviv service. Israir can market an American-operated flight as part of its own offering when American returns. An interline agreement will connect passengers beyond JFK. Travelers crossing the Atlantic on either airline will be able to combine that flight with American connections across the United States, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean. An interline agreement supplies the framework for selling a connecting trip on one ticket and through-checking bags. A codeshare adds another airline’s flight number to the same flight. The initial codeshare involves Israir marketing American’s flight. American hasn’t confirmed that it’s putting its code on Israir’s A330 service. Israir’s stock exchange filing claims the agreement was signed November 19, with initial implementation targeted by the end of 2026. That depends on regulatory approvals, technology and operational readiness. Israir Airbus A320, Credit: Oyoyoy via Wikimedia Commons Israir Sees A $20–40 Million Revenue Opportunity Until now, Israir’s New York route has competed primarily for passengers whose destination is New York. American connections let it compete for people going beyond New York as well. Israir estimates that this expands its potential customer market by 20–25%, creating an opportunity for $20–40 million in additional annual revenue. The filing though describes this as the larger addressable market rather than a revenue growth forecast. A codeshare on American’s flight also gives it something to sell when its own flight isn’t operating or its seats are full. For American, the near-term benefit is carrying Israir passengers on flights it’s already operating beyond JFK. Once American returns to Tel Aviv, Israir can also help sell seats on that flight through its own customer base and distribution in Israel. El Al And Delta Already Have A More Complete Partnership American is playing catch-up in Israel. Delta restored daily JFK–Tel Aviv service in September, and United returned that month as well. El Al and Arkia also serve the New York market. United can combine its Tel Aviv flying with its Newark hub. El Al has a Delta relationship that includes reciprocal codeshares, mileage earning and redemption, and elite benefits. That partnership began in 2024. What Passengers Get—And What They Don’t The immediate customer proposition is an easier connecting itinerary once the agreement goes live. Israir operates out of American’s JFK Terminal 8, so passengers won’t need to change terminals (and terminals aren’t connected airside at JFK). Passengers arriving from Israel still need to clear U.S. immigration and customs. Checking a bag through to the final destination doesn’t eliminate collecting and rechecking it on arrival in the United States. American also confirms Greenwich Lounge access at JFK for passengers flying Israir business class. However, there are no AAdvantage mileage earning, Loyalty Points, award redemptions or reciprocal elite benefits on Israir. The airlines say they’ll consider broader codesharing and AAdvantage benefits later. Hopefully status-earning and award redemption on Israir comes to fruition in the future.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, photo Credit: Griffith Observatory with downtown Los Angeles in the background.
    • A dozen cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties raised or updated lodging taxes in recent elections as cities prepare for a surge in visitors during the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
    • Five months after Los Angeles voters rejected an increase to the city’s lodging tax, the surrounding suburbs hiked their own.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, photo Credit: Griffith Observatory with downtown Los Angeles in the background. Wikimedia Commons / The Fun Chronicles.

    A dozen cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties raised or updated lodging taxes in recent elections as cities prepare for a surge in visitors during the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

    Five months after Los Angeles voters rejected an increase to the city’s lodging tax, the surrounding suburbs hiked their own.

    Preliminary results show 12 cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties approving changes to lodging taxes on November 3, according to the California Local Government Finance Almanac. Ten created or raised rates, with two cities pushing their hotel rates above Los Angeles’ 14% tax. Two expanded their current tax to cover more types of stays.

    The changes come as Los Angeles and the surrounding area prepare for a surge in visitation for the 2028 Olympics, which are expected to draw in roughly 2 million visitors to the greater Los Angeles area, and as local lawmakers work to address widening budget gaps. Skift previously reported that lodging taxes can be an easy sell because the people paying them aren’t usually locals who vote.

    In most cities, the increases are "not a huge amount of money compared to other sorts.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December.
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.
    • Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a recent development, rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

    The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

    Industry observers note that in a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

    “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver stated in her statement.

    Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

    Recent findings suggest that the August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, noted that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

    “We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

    It has been revealed that separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

    “I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

    In a recent development, ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

    The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

    In a recent development, court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

    According to recent reports, earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

    #54031. American Airlines Notes Operations Chief David Seymour Will Retire — With Dismissal-Style Severance

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4812 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    American Airlines Notes Operations Chief David Seymour Will Retire — With Dismissal-Style Severance

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines chief operating officer David Seymour is leaving the job December 31.
    • Seymour with the severance payments and benefits pursuant to the covered termination provisions set forth in his previously disclosed Severance Agreement with the Company dated as of September 20, 2023.
    • JonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson takes over January 1, reporting directly to Isom.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines chief operating officer David Seymour is leaving the job December 31. CEO Robert Isom calls it a retirement. The agreement American signed with Seymour gives him severance on terms normally reserved for dismissal without cause or resignation for good reason. American’s last proxy put the cash severance alone at $2,750,625 for a hypothetical departure on December 31, 2025, with total value over $7 million. The airline hasn’t disclosed the final amount for this exit. [T]he Company will provide Mr. Seymour with the severance payments and benefits pursuant to the covered termination provisions set forth in his previously disclosed Severance Agreement with the Company dated as of September 20, 2023.

    [T]he Manufacturer will provide Mr. Seymour with the severance payments and benefits pursuant to the covered termination provisions set forth in his previously disclosed Severance Agreement with the Company dated as of September 20, 2023.

    JonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson takes over January 1, reporting directly to Isom. He’s the executive I flagged as Seymour’s likely successor in August, when American handed him much of the job.

    In a recent development, aviation watchdog JonNYC shared Isom’s message to employees. Isom thanks Seymour for his friendship and his work bringing US Airways and American together. Before joining America West in 1999, Seymour led a platoon in the 82nd Airborne. Just last month he went back to West Point and Fort Bragg with Medal of Honor recipients to meet the cadets and soldiers who followed him there.

    AA pic.twitter.com/9919XVOKrW — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 20, 2026.

    In a recent development, under Seymour’s contract, cash severance is 18 months of salary plus a year and a half of target bonus. He also gets money for 18 months of health premiums, and his stock can keep vesting during those 18 months. Between cash, stock, health premiums and flight benefits he’d already earned, American’s illustration in its latest proxy came to $7.13 million. Separately, Seymour remains eligible for his 2026 annual bonus. His advisory job pays $25,000 a month for up to three months ($75,000), plus executive benefits. His contract calculates severance using pay immediately before termination. Seymour has to sign a release and honor his existing restrictions, and American says it’ll file the full transition letter with its annual report. Those flight benefits include lifetime confirmed personal travel in any cabin for Seymour and his immediate family, Admirals Club access and another 12 confirmed roundtrips a year for friends and other relatives. The Handoff Started In August When American put Heather Garboden in charge of the customer experience, they gave her two bosses. She was supposed to persuade customers to pay more to fly American while reporting both to commercial and to the executive responsible for getting flights off the gate on time. When a pilot asked Seymour in 2022 what American was doing about poor customer satisfaction, his answer was “I think we’re on a good path to get there.” He went on to talk about running the operation. What was Garboden supposed to do when the catering truck was late and the choice was a delayed departure or six hours in first class without meals? In August Garboden began reporting solely to chief commercial officer Nat Pieper and picked up catering, reservations and service recovery. Pieper also got marketing, brand, advertising and partnerships as American broke up Global Engagement head Ron DeFeo’s group. Caroline Clayton took corporate communications. Then I reported network chief Brian Znotins was leaving as Pieper set out to rebuild flying in big cities where American had pulled back. Seymour actually picked up American Eagle in August. But Gulbranson got the airports and operations planning on top of flight operations, flight attendants and the control center. Now he gets safety, regulatory compliance and aircraft maintenance, too. Corporate security goes to government affairs chief Steve Neuman. American will tell employees in December who gets the regionals. If this hadn’t actually been decided already, then August was Gulbranson’s audition. Isom’s memo introduces the retirement as the next step in the August reorganization. Seymour’s contract even lists a material reduction in responsibilities as grounds that can qualify an executive for severance. We don’t know who first proposed retirement, but this looks to me like a negotiated handoff that was already well underway. American Had To Retrofit Planes It Had Just Retrofitted While there are numerous stories like it – such as insufficient oversight of outsourced Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul – I always think of a few things about Seymour’s tenure. One is explaining why the airline wouldn’t invest in RFID baggage tags like Delta despite perpetually bottom of the industry performance in mishandled bags. Another is failing to fix ‘Concept D’ business class seats that rocked. And the biggest is mismanaging cabin retrofits of the domestic fleet. Seymour was running integrated operations when the first American Airlines 737 MAX introduced the cabin that would go into its existing 737s and Airbus A321s. A flight attendant eventually asked whether anyone had built a mockup before committing to it. They hadn’t. Doug Parker stated network planning had largely driven the design. Seymour called it “a mistake that should not have happened” and later explained what American had changed. For subsequent cabins they’d bring in real seats, build overhead bins and try pushing a service cart through. In his words, “We do mockups and not just you know ‘tape it out.’” Flight attendants working in the back galley had to help passengers get out of the lavatories because the two doors opened into each other and caught. The sinks were too shallow for the water pressure. I washed my hands on the inaugural flight and got water all over my shirt and pants, as did everyone else. Up front, the seat supports took up the space where a first class passenger was supposed to put a bag. American was still installing the interior after deciding to fix it. Project Oasis put the newly introduced seats into existing 737s. Then Project Kodiak went back into planes they’d already redone to fix the storage, give the first row some legroom back and add the device holders coach passengers already had. How Well Did American Actually Run? After the troubled summer of 2019, American gave Seymour responsibility for all operations. The following June he got the chief operating officer title and added flight service. For years my frustration was that when the operation fell short, the answer seemed to be to give the executive running it a bigger job. In 2023 American completed its highest share of scheduled flights since the merger and edged out United on domestic on-time arrivals. And spreading the Dallas schedule from nine daily rushes to 13 smaller ones helped passengers this year. The hub chief reported half as many missed connections in the first 17 days. But by 2025 American ranked eighth of ten network airlines for on-time arrivals. And the Transportation Department’s new figures show that Delta and United both beat American every single month from January through September 2026. Counting domestic flights including regional partners, American came in at 73.30% on time, United at 76.20% and Delta at 78.31%. American canceled 46,059 flights, or 2.99% of its schedule, against 1.75% at United and 2.25% at Delta. Credit: American Airlines One clue to what management valued is in that same proxy. In August 2025 the board gave Seymour a retention stock award worth about $2 million at target. The entire award turns on avoiding cancellations American counts as controllable. A flight that runs three hours late still counts as a success on that measure. The award measures performance through June 2027, so it can still pay out after he’s gone. Gulbranson is well regarded inside American. He started at Northwest, joined US Airways in 2008 and helped integrate flight operations systems during the merger. He’s run both the control center that decides what to cancel and the customer care operation that hears from the people who get stranded. Credit: American Airlines Listen to the two men describe January’s Winter Storm Fern. Seymour said the technology worked as intended and that he hadn’t seen reports of flight attendants sleeping in airports even as his boss Isom acknowledged crew had slept on floors. Gulbranson went before the pilots’ union board and told them where management had misjudged the storm and overestimated how swiftly they could recover. The union’s account called his assessment “unvarnished.” That’s one reason I’m glad he’ll be running the operation the next time it snows in Dallas and up the East Coast.     • Denver airport’s top lawyer has spent eight months on paid leave, collecting a salary of roughly $225,000 a year.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Denver airport’s top lawyer has spent eight months on paid leave, collecting a salary of roughly $225,000 a year. Now Denver wants a federal judge to let it fire him. But the airport’s general counsel Everett Martinez states city officials retaliated against him for raising legal objections to their improper dealings and for refusing to help push out airport CEO Phil Washington. The city says he violated his professional obligations and wants to stop paying someone who can’t perform the job. Meanwhile, Denver has authorized up to $970,000 for outside lawyers handling his case and a separate employment lawsuit. The $470,000 budget for the first phase of his case is quite an expense for a fight between the city and its own airport lawyer. I’ve called Denver the worst airport in the country. It can work reasonably well as a connecting hub. Actually getting to and from Denver, through the terminal and out to a gate is another matter. This latest fight brings together several of the reasons the place inspires so little confidence: political interference, weak financial oversight, and executives spending their time fighting each other. The city’s November 10 filing argues keeping Martinez on leave is harming Denver during a budget crisis. Martinez wants paid leave to continue while he litigates, potentially for years. At approximately $225,000 annually, eight months works out to about $150,000 in salary, before benefits. That’s arithmetic, rather than a payroll accounting. The distinction between airport money and city money matters here. His salary is airport money. Martinez’s complaint says it comes entirely from the airport’s enterprise fund. That’s separate from Denver’s general fund. Airport revenue consists of things like airline rents and landing fees, parking and concession. That’s not money that can get moved to the city’s programs anyway. The outside defense contract is budgeted to city money. The council’s contract worksheet identifies the general fund as its funding source. So it’s actually the city that’s draining funds amidst a budget crisis, although it’s possible they try to bill it back to the airport. The $970,000 covers two cases. The city’s budget presentation allocates $470,000 to the first phase of Martinez’s case and $500,000 to a separate case. They’re authorizing spending ‘up to’ this amount at this stage. The amended agreement sets rates of $800 an hour for attorneys and $375 for paralegals. The firm is Wheeler Trigg O’Donnell, where city attorney Miko Brown previously worked. Funny that. Brown says a five-person panel considered four firms and unanimously selected this one, which Denver had used since 2011. She says she cast her vote for her former firm last. Martinez alleges he was punished after objecting to the Park Hill Golf Course land swap, warning against withholding information from federal aviation officials, and resisting pressure to help remove Washington. He also alleges discriminatory treatment and an ugly remark from Brown suggesting he get a noose. The city denies his allegations. The city didn’t want to lease airport space to a carrier involved in ICE deportation flights and Martinez wasn’t helpful in covering this up (it’s against the law). I coverde the Key Lime Air affair last year. Then I covered a memo supporting Martinez’s account that officials subsequently sought to manufacture a safety justification for the decision. The memo was written before his lawsuit, and another airport executive endorsed its accuracy. The Federal Aviation Administration opened a formal investigation into the lease denial with $90 million in federal grants at risk. Additionally, the city wanted airport property for a park. There are federal restrictions involved in transferrin ghte land. Martinez appears to have stood in the way (likely as he was obligated to). But the city has counterclaimed for breach of fiduciary duty, conversion and civil theft. Martinez may have a legitimate employment claim but that doesn’t give him the right to remain on the payroll throughout the litigation. He says his first amendment rights are being violated, but the Supreme Court generally doesn’t treat speech made pursuant to an employee’s official duties as protected citizen speech and giving the city legal advice was his job. And while he ostensibly also helped protect then-airport CEO Phil Washington, it’s not at all clear that Washington was doing a good job. (He retired August 1.) I covered Washington’s nomination to lead the Federal Aviation Administration and its collapse. He’d spent less than two years running an airport after a career in the military and public transit. During his confirmation hearing, he couldn’t answer a series of seven aviation questions from Senator Ted Budd. And his actual airport record is spotty. Construction oversight. A 2023 audit of the Great Hall project identified inadequate contractor oversight, procurement concerns and overcharges. The January 2025 follow-up found only two of ten recommendations for improvement fully implemented, and no corrective action on seven items. The construction debacle predated Washington, but I view his record as overall quite bad on accountability. Concession revenue. After an audit found weaknesses in rent collection and monitoring concessionaire deductions, the airport accepted 13 recommendations. By October 2025, only three were fully implemented. Accounting problems continued. Executive travel. I wrote about the extraordinary airfare bills for a Madrid conference. The ethics board’s written decision lists $12,047.01 for Washington’s airfare and $19,194.21 for his chief operating officer. My hunch is they were running for MileagePlus status. The board dismissed the ethics complaint for insufficient evidence of private gain, while sharply criticizing the spending and Washington’s response. His ‘need to be ready-to-work-on-arrival’ justification looked weak when he arrived three days before being on the program. The trains remain a good illustration of the airport’s deeper problem. I covered 131 breakdowns over a year. Most interruptions were brief. But passengers still lack a walking alternative to the B and C concourses. Denver is finally planning pedestrian routes through existing baggage tunnels, estimated at $300 million to $700 million, with completion expected in 2028 or 2029. That’s where I’d like to see the airport’s management attention go. Instead, airport consumers are paying a sidelined general counsel, city taxpayers are funding the defense against him, and the people responsible for running the place are arguing over whether their own lawyer can be trusted.     Sabre spent years modernizing its shopping, booking, and servicing systems for AI applications to use. Now it's pursuing the major AI platforms themselves, aiming to keep travel transactions flowing through its systems even as the customer relationship moves elsewhere.

    In a recent development, sabre's upcoming Mosaic Travel Connector for Grok Bot is the latest step. Declared this week and still in private beta, it is designed to bring flight and hotel shopping, booking, and servicing into the AI assistant.

    The stakes are high for airlines and hotels. AI assistants could send them customers without travelers ever visiting their websites, but the platforms could also decide which handful of offers consumers see.

    Recent findings suggest that sabre CEO Kurt Ekert explained why that matters: "the consumer will not paginate through results. They're going to get back one, two, maybe three options and choose from that.".

    Trump Indicates His Private Pilot Used To Use Foreign Air Traffic Control Because The American System Is So Bad

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that donald Trump indicates his private pilot used another country’s air traffic control because the American system was so bad.
    • Sources indicate that pilots don’t get that choice.
    • At his Friday press conference, Trump noted his “pilot would use the air traffic control from a totally different country.” This was supposedly before his first term, 11 or 12 years ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that donald Trump indicates his private pilot used another country’s air traffic control because the American system was so bad. He wouldn’t identify the country, as though his pilot had discovered a better provider for approaches into Teterboro and didn’t want everyone else signing up. Pilots don’t get that choice. And this isn’t just an ambiguous reference to flying overseas. Trump has made this claim before and described landing in New York, Florida and Tennessee. At his Friday press conference, Trump said his “pilot would use the air traffic control from a totally different country.” This was supposedly before his first term, 11 or 12 years ago. Then he declared, “I know a lot about air traffic control.” Watch Trump describe his pilot using another country’s air traffic control — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar), November 20, 2026 Air traffic control assigns clearances and separates aircraft sharing the same airspace. The controller responsible for your flight changes as you move between sectors and facilities. Your pilot can request a different route or altitude. They can reject an unsafe instruction. They can’t decide to use a different country’s air traffic control service because they like it better. And there’s a clear division of responsibilities. Pilots fly the aircraft and request changes to clearances when needed. Controllers coordinate the traffic. Could There Be A Real Story Behind This? I’ve tried to come up with something plausible, to create the most generous interpretation of these remarks. The best I can do is that Trump is confusing navigation equipment with air traffic control. Perhaps his pilot told him about a preferred navigation system, approach procedure or a piece of equipment he liked from overseas, and that became a story about choosing another country’s controllers. There are also real circumstances where an American flight uses foreign air traffic services: Crossing the North Atlantic. A flight to Scotland could pass through airspace handled by Nav Canada’s Gander operation and Britain’s Shanwick operation. Taking a route through Canada. A pilot could request a route that avoids congested U.S. sectors and spends more time in Canadian airspace (but it doesn’t give Canadian controllers responsibility for a landing in Tennessee). Flying in U.S. airspace assigned to Canadian controllers. “American airspace means American controllers” isn’t always true. Under a 1963 agreement, the United States delegates control of certain portions of its airspace within 50 nautical miles of the Canadian border. But the government assigned that responsibility, the pilot doesn’t choose their preferred controller. None of this would reconcile his comments with what he claimed on May 8, 2025.     #54023. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (942 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
    • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
    • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

    Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

    The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

    Sources indicate that the power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

    In a recent development, it’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller stated that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

    Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

    "When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller said.

    A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

    “The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide remarked.

    In a recent development, king is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

    Industry observers note that last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

    While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

    The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

    In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

    And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

    Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

    The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

    As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

    The relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

    That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

    A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

    “We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling said.

    The bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

    But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

    Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

    Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

    • Photo Credit: The Riyadh Skyline Wikimedia Commons / B.alotaby.
    • According to recent reports, riyadh’s hotels lost their peak season when the airport shut.
    • According to recent reports, riyadh hotels had one of their worst months of the year in October.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Photo Credit: The Riyadh Skyline Wikimedia Commons / B.alotaby.

    According to recent reports, riyadh’s hotels lost their peak season when the airport shut. With BA, Cathay Pacific and others suspended into the newly introduced year and Houthi strikes still hitting the capital, the recovery hasn’t started.

    According to recent reports, riyadh hotels had one of their worst months of the year in October. A temporary shutdown of the city’s main airport cut off inbound demand just as peak season started.

    Industry observers note that occupancy fell 34.7 percentage points year over year to 34.3% from 69%, according to CoStar’s STR. Only March had lower occupancy, at 28.3%. Average daily rate dropped 29.9% to $190 and revenue per available room (RevPAR) fell 65.1% to $65.

    “October and November are usually the peak season months for Riyadh, so the impact is much bigger,” noted Kostas Nikolaidis, associate account director for Middle East and Africa at STR.

    The October demand collapse traces back to an attack on King Khalid International Airport. The airport closed after an attack on Oct. 10 that Saudi authorities mentioned killed 13 people and injured more than 300. Some 86% of scheduled Riyadh departures were canceled between Oct. 8 and late October, according to Cirium data, Skift repor.

    Mexico’s President Spent 21 Hours In Coach Getting To China—And Sat In A Middle Seat

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3207 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines.
    • That’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar.
    • It has been revealed that the 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines. She reportedly sat in 33B. A middle seat, on a trip across the Pacific, to represent her country at a summit of world leaders. That’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar. But while Sheinbaum is winning praise for saving taxpayers money, she should have flown business class. The 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Here’s her departure enhancement: Claudia Sheinbaum’s update on her trip to Shenzhen, November 15, 2026 21 Hours Includes The Stop In Tijuana She left Mexico City early Sunday, November 15, on China Southern flight CZ8032 and arrived in Shenzhen on Monday. The Airbus A350-900 made its scheduled technical stop in Tijuana along the way. The first flight took 3 hours 12 minutes and the transpacific segment clocked in at 14 hours 56 minutes, with about two and a half hours on the ground between them. China Southern operates the route nonstop from Shenzhen to Mexico City, with the Tijuana stop in the other direction. Several stories report that seat 33B is in the back of the aircraft. In fact, it’s the front of standard economy. On arrival she posted video of her welcome in Shenzhen. An airport bus brought her to the red carpet, where an honor guard and performers waited. She received a presidential welcome. Which reminds me a little bit of when I’ve booked first class awards on Lufthansa, but the intra-European segment was only available in coach. Nobody ever could quite figure out how a coach passenger had a vehicle waiting for them on the tarmac. She returned on China Southern flight CZ8031 and shared a photo with the crew: Claudia Sheinbaum thanks the crew of flight CZ8031 on her return from Shenzhen Mexico Sold Its Presidential 787 Sheinbaum is continuing a practice established by Andrés Manuel López Obrador. In July 2020, I wrote about Mexico’s president flying Delta coach and connecting in Atlanta to meet Trump. He had an exit row aisle seat on a Delta flight from Mexico City. Delta was blocking middle seats at the time, too, due to the pandemic. Reforma’s video of López Obrador boarding Delta for his Washington trip, July 7, 2020 López Obrador refused to use Mexico’s presidential Boeing 787-8. After years of trying to find a buyer, Mexico sold it to Tajikistan for about $92 million in 2023. He said the proceeds would fund two hospitals. This isn’t Sheinbaum’s first long trip in coach, either. In April I covered her economy trip to Europe, flying through Madrid to Barcelona and returning to Mexico City on Aeromexico. She posted a photo of herself working at her coach seat: Claudia Sheinbaum working during her April 2026 trip to Barcelona I thought that was performative then. A president’s time has value, and so does being rested for the work the country is sending her to do. Aeromexico business class would have provided better rest and opportunity to work. Pringles, Princes, And A Qatari 747 I’ve covered plenty of politicians and royals flying coach. Prince William flew American Airlines economy from Memphis to Dallas in 2014, in a bulkhead window seat on an Airbus A319. He’s also flown Ryanair and taken the family on Flybe, carrying their hand luggage. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle flew British Airways coach to Nice for Upcoming Year’s in 2017. They and three bodyguards occupied the last three rows, with empty seats around them. T Argentina’s Javier Milei flew coach on his trip to Davos in January 2024. Given Argentina’s finances and the spending cuts he wanted the public to accept, there was a political purpose for the symbolism. David Cameron was photographed eating Pringles and working on his iPad aboard easyJet in 2015, while traveling to Portugal. I liked that one. William and Harry’s grandfather Prince Philip, though, described the improvements in air travel over his lifetime with the qualification, “provided you don’t travel in something called economy class, which sounds ghastly.” Meanwhile, thhe Pentagon accepted Qatar’s Boeing 747-8 in May 2025 for Trump’s use as Air Force One. It was widely described as a $400 million gift. I covered the Qatari jet’s conversion this summer, including the decision to preserve its luxury interior and the plan for it eventually to go to Trump’s presidential library. The U.S. president needs secure communications, protection, and the ability to keep working while traveling. That can justify dedicated aircraft. Sheinbaum’s coach trip earned publicity, including favorable attention in China while she was there to meet its leaders. But saving the difference between coach and business class is simply a poor value tradeoff when the cost is productive time and sleep for someone with a high opportunity cost.
